explanations.explanation: That's what Abraham says of his wife Sarah while he's staying in Gerar (Genesis 20:2). Four little words, and this chapter is off and running. Abimelech, king of Gerar, is about to hear them, and I think things are about to get complicated for him.

Servant? Friend, that's a WILD word to use about your wife. Abraham doesn't say it. He says of Sarah, “She is my sister.” (Genesis 20:2) And he says it in a place where a king is about to take notice, so that line is carrying a lot.
Cousin never comes out of Abraham's mouth in this passage. What he says is “She is my sister.” (Genesis 20:2) Later in the chapter he explains himself, so hang on to that thought, friend.
Abimelech, the king of Gerar, had Sarah brought to him (Genesis 20:2). The text says it plainly and moves on. That's one of those moments where the reader leans toward the page and says, uh oh.

Nobody gets walked to the border here. The text says Abimelech had Sarah brought to him (Genesis 20:2), so the king's move is about Sarah, not Abraham's exit. I think Abraham is standing there holding his breath. And a dream is headed the king's way that very night (Genesis 20:3).

No prison shows up anywhere in this passage. Abimelech's move is to have Sarah brought to him (Genesis 20:2). Abraham is never locked up. Later Abimelech gives him sheep, cattle, menservants and maidservants (Genesis 20:14), and I think that's a strange gift to hand a prisoner.

God tells Abimelech, “You are as good as dead because of the woman you have taken, for she is a married woman.” (Genesis 20:3) That's a heavy thing to hear, even in a dream. I bet Abimelech's eyes were wide open the whole time he was asleep.
Sarah isn't a widow. Her husband Abraham is alive and well, and God says “…she is a married woman.” (Genesis 20:3) That word is the whole reason for the warning.
God doesn't use that word about Sarah here. What He says is that she is “…a married woman.” (Genesis 20:3) And that's exactly why Abimelech is in trouble.
Abimelech says, “Lord, would You destroy a nation even though it is innocent?” (Genesis 20:4) He doesn't just sit there quietly. He answers God right in the middle of the dream.
This one is true, friend. Abimelech did ask God a question: “Lord, would You destroy a nation even though it is innocent?” (Genesis 20:4) He speaks up even while he's dreaming.
Abimelech says Sarah herself said, “He is my brother.” (Genesis 20:5) So both of them told him the same thing, and he points to that as part of his defense. Honestly, he's got his paperwork in order.
Abimelech never says Sarah called Abraham her master. He says she told him, “He is my brother.” (Genesis 20:5) Brother matches what Abraham said about her.
Guardian isn't what Abimelech reports. He says Sarah herself said, “He is my brother.” (Genesis 20:5) Her words lined up with Abraham's, and Abimelech brings that up right away.
God tells him, “Yes, I know that you did this with a clear conscience…” (Genesis 20:6) God doesn't brush off what Abimelech said. He answers him directly, still in the dream.
The text says the opposite, friend. God tells Abimelech, “Yes, I know that you did this with a clear conscience…” (Genesis 20:6) God answers him right there in the dream.
God says it Himself: “That is why I did not let you touch her.” (Genesis 20:6) He also says He kept Abimelech from sinning against Him. So the stopping was God's doing, start to finish.
Sarah's words aren't what God points to here. Abimelech says she told him, “He is my brother.” (Genesis 20:5) The reason God gives is this: “That is why I did not let you touch her.” (Genesis 20:6)
The text never shows Abraham stepping in. God says, “…I have kept you from sinning against Me. That is why I did not let you touch her.” (Genesis 20:6) The One doing the keeping is God.

Prophet is it, baker. God tells Abimelech, “…for he is a prophet; he will pray for you and you will live.” (Genesis 20:7) Notice who is getting called a prophet: Abraham, the same man who just got caught in a mess. God still names him that, and God still has him pray for the king.
God says, “he will pray for you and you will live.” (Genesis 20:7) The prayer is how Abimelech lives. And later in the chapter, Abraham does exactly that (Genesis 20:17).
King is Abimelech's job, not Abraham's. God calls Abraham “a prophet” (Genesis 20:7). Abimelech is the one wearing the crown in Gerar.
Nobody picks up a sword in this story. God says Abraham “…will pray for you and you will live.” (Genesis 20:7) The help here comes through prayer.

God doesn't use servant in this verse. He says Abraham “…is a prophet…” (Genesis 20:7). That's the title God gives him, and it comes right before God says Abraham will pray for Abimelech so that he lives.
This one is false, friend. God says, “…be aware that you will surely die—you and all who belong to you.” (Genesis 20:7) It isn't just Abimelech on the line. His whole household is in it with him.

That's right, it isn't only Abimelech. God says, “…be aware that you will surely die—you and all who belong to you.” (Genesis 20:7) The warning covers his whole household, and that's a big reason to listen.

The text says the men were terrified (Genesis 20:8). Abimelech tells them all that happened, and they don't take it lightly. I think a boss telling you his dream shouldn't normally scare you, but this one did.
Nobody is thrilled in that room. The text says the men were terrified (Genesis 20:8). God's warning had just reached them too.
Doubt isn't what the text shows. When Abimelech describes everything to his servants, the men were terrified (Genesis 20:8). They take it seriously right away.

Abimelech says Abraham has brought “…such tremendous guilt upon me and my kingdom?” (Genesis 20:9) He's talking about his whole kingdom, not just himself. That's a lot of weight to carry out of a dream.
Famine isn't what Abimelech says. He says Abraham has brought “…such tremendous guilt upon me and my kingdom?” (Genesis 20:9) The trouble he's talking about is guilt.
Abimelech isn't talking about money here. His words are “…such tremendous guilt upon me and my kingdom?” (Genesis 20:9) I think that word tells you how heavy it feels to him.

Abraham says, “Surely there is no fear of God in this place.” (Genesis 20:11) That's what he tells Abimelech he thought to himself. He follows it with, “They will kill me on account of my wife.” (Genesis 20:11) So the worry he names is about his own life.

Altar isn't the word. Abraham says, “Surely there is no fear of God in this place.” (Genesis 20:11) He's telling Abimelech what he figured about the people of Gerar, and it was a guess on his part. He follows it with, “They will kill me on account of my wife.” (Genesis 20:11) So the worry he names is about his own life.

Abraham doesn't say love. His words are “Surely there is no fear of God in this place.” (Genesis 20:11) That's what he tells Abimelech he thought to himself, and fear of God is the thing he says he didn't expect to find. Then he adds, “They will kill me on account of my wife.” (Genesis 20:11)

explanations.answer: Kill him because of his wife
explanations.explanation: Abraham says he thought, “They will kill me on account of my wife.” (Genesis 20:11) That's his reason, in his own words. He tells Abimelech straight out.
Abraham doesn't mention flocks or herds as his worry. He says, “They will kill me on account of my wife.” (Genesis 20:11) His fear was about his life.

explanations.answer: Drive him out of the land
explanations.explanation: Being driven out isn't what Abraham says he feared. His words are “They will kill me on account of my wife.” (Genesis 20:11) That's a much bigger worry than a moving truck.
It's the other way around, friend. Abraham says Sarah is “…the daughter of my father—though not the daughter of my mother…” (Genesis 20:12) Same father, different mother.

Right, it's flipped. Abraham says, “…she really is my sister, the daughter of my father—though not the daughter of my mother—and she became my wife.” (Genesis 20:12) So she's his father's daughter, not his mother's.

Loyalty is the word, baker. Abraham tells the king what he asked of Sarah: “This is how you can show your loyalty to me…” (Genesis 20:13) He's explaining himself after the fact, and he ties it back to when God had him journey from his father's house. Explaining yourself after the fact is a skill I know well, friend. I've done it over a tray of crumbs.

Courage isn't what Abraham says. He asks Sarah, “This is how you can show your loyalty to me…” (Genesis 20:13) Loyalty is about sticking with him, not about being brave. The thing he asks her to say is that he's her brother, wherever they go.
Abraham doesn't talk about wisdom here. He says, “This is how you can show your loyalty to me…” (Genesis 20:13) It's a request about loyalty, wherever they go.
The text says Abimelech brought “…sheep and cattle, menservants and maidservants…” and gave them to Abraham (Genesis 20:14). He restored Sarah too. That's quite a gift on top of giving his wife back.

This one is true, friend. Abimelech brought “…sheep and cattle, menservants and maidservants…” and gave them to Abraham, and he restored Sarah to him (Genesis 20:14). Abraham ends up with more than he had.

Abimelech says, “Look, my land is before you. Settle wherever you please.” (Genesis 20:15) That's a wide-open invitation from a king. It comes right after he gives Abraham sheep, cattle and servants and restores Sarah to him (Genesis 20:14).
There's no deadline in the text. Abimelech says, “Look, my land is before you. Settle wherever you please.” (Genesis 20:15) The door is open, not shut.
Abimelech doesn't put anything off limits. His words are “Look, my land is before you. Settle wherever you please.” (Genesis 20:15) He gives Abraham the choice.
Abimelech tells Sarah, “It is your vindication before all who are with you; you are completely cleared.” (Genesis 20:16) The silver comes with those words. He says it right to her.
Honored guest isn't what Abimelech says. He tells Sarah, “It is your vindication before all who are with you; you are completely cleared.” (Genesis 20:16) That's the meaning he gives the silver.

Abimelech doesn't talk about protection here. He tells Sarah, “It is your vindication before all who are with you; you are completely cleared.” (Genesis 20:16) The silver is about clearing her name in front of everyone with her. Guarding her isn't what he says.

The text says the LORD “…had completely closed all the wombs in Abimelech’s household.” on account of Sarah (Genesis 20:18). That's why they needed healing after Abraham prayed (Genesis 20:17). It's a heavy detail, so I'll just say it plainly and leave it there.
The text doesn't mention the flocks being sick. It says the LORD “…had completely closed all the wombs in Abimelech’s household.” (Genesis 20:18) That's what the healing was for.

Nobody is struck blind in this passage. The text says the LORD “…had completely closed all the wombs in Abimelech’s household.” on account of Sarah (Genesis 20:18). And Abraham's prayer is what brought the healing (Genesis 20:17).
